newsitem.title: INDIA: TEXT-Statement by India's SEBI on takeovers, FIIs.
newsitem.headline: TEXT-Statement by India's SEBI on takeovers, FIIs.

text.p: The following is a full text of a statement issued by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Thursday on takeovers, foreign institutional investment in gilts and other related issues:

In a liberalised environment requiring greater transparency, efficiency and investor protection, there is a need for evolving a well defined and orderly framework for takeovers and substantial acquisition of shares. Recognising this need, the SEBI Board considered the Report of the Bhagwati Committee on Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers and approved the Report and the draft Regulations with certain modifications.
SALIENT FEATURES ARE GIVEN BELOW:
** Mandatory public offer is triggered off when-
+ the threshold limit of 10 percent is crossed;
+ there is change in control

** For the purpose of consolidation of holdings, acquirers holding not less than 10 percent but not more than 51 percent are allowed 'creeping acquisition' upto 2 percent in any period of 12 months. Any purchase by a person holding more than 51 percent would have to be in a transparent manner, through a public tender offer.

** The definition of "control" proposed in the draft Regulations would be suitably modified to make the definition more precise and comprehensive and to ensure that shareholder democracy is not compromised in any way. This will also form one of the guiding principles of the regulations.

** An acquirer, including persons presently in control of the company, should make a public offer to acquire a minimum of 20 percent in case the conditions for mandatory public offer mentioned earlier is attracted. It was felt that in view of lack of availability of bank finance or any other external source of finance at present, the public offer was restricted to 20 percent instead of 100 percent.

** SEBI would not be involved in pricing of offer, which is essentially a market function. Pricing will be based on the parameters such as the negotiated price, average of the high and low price for 26 weeks period before the date of the public announcement, highest price paid by the acquirer for any acquisition during the 26 weeks period before the date of the public announcement and the price for preferential offers if any.

** Definitions of 'acquirer' and 'persons acting in concert' have been amplified to cover direct as well as indirect acquisition, through acquisition of investment or holding companies, and also acquisition of control of the company without acquisition of shares.
** The concept of 'Chain Principle' has been introduced, requiring public offer to be made to shareholders of each company when several companies are acquired through acquisition of one company.
** Regulations are made applicable essentially for secondary market transactions.
** Cases where the Regulations are made inapplicable have been spelt out, thus bringing clarity and transparency.

** On cases requiring grant of exemption, SEBI would be guided by the recommendations of a Panel to be set up. The composition of the Panel would comprise majority of independent persons capable of giving impartial and objective legal opinion.
SEBI NOT INVOLVED IN PRICING ..

** As mentioned earlier, SEBI would not be involved in pricing of the offer. Besides, by delineating cases where the Regulations are made inapplicable and by setting up a Panel for considering cases for exemption, use of discretion by SEBI would be reduced to the bare minimum.

** Disclosure requirement has been strengthened requiring disclosure of additional details such as financial arrangements in place for implementing the offer, whether the acquirer intends to strip or otherwise encumber the assets of the target company, other than in the ordinary course of business, future plans of the acquirer for the target company etc. Further, disclosure of misleading information and non-disclosure of material information would be deemed a violation attracting penal action.

** Conditional offer has been allowed subject to either minimum mandatory acceptance of 20 percent with differential pricing; or with a deposit of 50 percent of the value of the offer in cash in the escrow, in cases where the bidder does not want to be saddled with the 20 percent acquisition. This, while checking frivolous conditional offers, will also permit flexibility to the genuine acquirer.

** The obligations of the board of target company have been spelt out. In particular, during the offer period, the board of the target company is precluded from inducting into the board any person belonging to the acquirer or transfer shares in their name till after completion of all formalities relating to the offer.
** Additional obligations have been cast on the merchant banker and non-exercise of due diligence by them on takeover issues would attract penal provisions.

** Penalty provisions have been strengthened, such as increasing the scope of cooling period to cover bid for any listed company for one year for non-fulfillment of obligations by the acquirer, forfeiture of escrow, requiring payment of interest to the shareholders for delay in payment of consideration, prohibiting entry into the board of the target during the offer period etc.
The Board also recognised that given the rapidly changing

economic environment in the country, regulations on a subject as complex as substantial acquisitions of shares and takeovers cannot be considered to be fixed and immutable. Regulations of this nature will have to keep pace with changing social and economic matrix and the emerging global scenario for otherwise, they will tend to strangulate growth and development in the country.
Necessary steps are being taken by SEBI to notify the Regulations as early as possible.
AMENDMENTS TO SEBI REGULATIONS FOR FOREIGN INSTITUTIONAL
INVESTORS:-
- It was decided to:

* permit FIIs to invest in dated Government securities within the framework of guidelines on FII investment in debt instruments for 100 percent debt funds, subject to an annual cap on such investments within the overall external commercial borrowing cap for the year, and

* permit Proprietary Funds to invest through the FII route provided such funds belong to the FIIs and subject to the condition that these FIIs are regulated by their home regulators or are registered with their tax authorities.

It was also decided that the requirement for FIIs or sub accounts of FIIs to be broad based would be removed. This would facilitate investment by pilot funds or seed funds which aim to establish a track record prior to wide distribution of these funds. The above changes to the regulations will soon come into effect with the notification of the amendments to the SEBI (Foreign Institutional Investors) Regulations, 1995.
USE OF iNDICATIVE RETURNS BY MUTUAL FUNDS:
Schemes launched by Mutual Funds would be allowed to mention an indicative return for schemes for fixed income securities with the following disclosures:

* The scheme should mention in the offer documents and advertisements that the returns are based on the current yield of instruments which may change from time to time depending upon the interest rates prevailing in the market, RBI policy and other relevant factors.
* In case a portfolio of securities is disclosed, it should also be mentioned that such a portfolio is a hypothetical example and the scheme does not assure that it would maintain this portfolio.

* The returns mentioned are only indicative and not assured and the actual returns that would be available to an unitholder will be based on the actual NAV which may go up or down depending on the market conditions.
The above disclosures will have to be made in large fonts and should appear immediately after the mention of the indicative returns so that investors attention is easily drawn.
SEBI ON SHAH REPORT:
B.D. Shah Committee Report on Short Selling and Securities Lending:

The Board considered the B.D. Shah Committee Report on Short Selling and decided that the earlier decision of the board on declaration of scrip wise net Short Sale position would continue. Similarly declaration of scrip wise net long purchase position would also be introduced. As decided earlier, short sale would not be prohibited but only regulated through imposition of margins. As regards margins, the Stock Exchanges would be given flexibility to impose the margins in consultation with SEBI on long buyers and short sellers depending on market conditions.

B.D. Shah Committee's recommendations on securities lending were also discussed and approved by the Board. In terms of the Scheme, the lenders will deposit the securities with an approved intermediary under an agreement for a specified period and the agreement shall provide that the beneficial interest shall continue to remain with the lender and all the corporate benefits shall continue to accrue to the lender. The approved intermediary should have a minimum networth of 500 million rupees.
The Board also reviewed recent trend in the Primary Market, Secondary Market, Mutual Funds and FII investments; as well as recent price movements.
PRIMARY MARKET:

The Board also agreed to review the existing Guidelines for Disclosure and Investor Protection to provide that any investor applying for securities in a public issue upto 200 securities will be given priority in allotment.
